title: Why Do We Sleep?
paragraphs: That humans spend roughly a third of their existence asleep has long posed a scientific conundrum: an organism would hardly evolve to surrender so much time to unconsciousness without compelling reasons. Contemporary consensus among sleep researchers and public health authorities holds that adults need between seven and nine hours a night, and that children and adolescents, whose neural development is still under way, require considerably more.

Far from being a monolithic state of quiescence, sleep unfolds as a sequence of cycles lasting approximately ninety minutes. Within each, the sleeper descends from light sleep into deep, slow-wave sleep before entering REM sleep, a stage distinguished by rapid eye movements and by the vivid, often narrative dreams with which it is most closely associated.

The stages seem to fulfil complementary functions. Slow-wave sleep is implicated in physical restoration and in memory consolidation, whereby labile new memories are stabilised and woven into existing knowledge networks. Animal studies have additionally demonstrated that the clearance of metabolic waste from the brain accelerates markedly during sleep, a finding that hints at a neuroprotective role, though its full significance for humans remains a subject of ongoing inquiry.

An isolated night of poor sleep is of little lasting consequence, yet sustained deprivation exacts a demonstrable cost: attention, memory and judgement erode, emotional regulation falters, and habitual short sleep correlates with heightened risk across a spectrum of health conditions. Sleep, then, is best understood not as idle downtime but as an active, indispensable process underpinning much of what we do while awake.
